newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stopped strike to avoid air travel chaos.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stopped strike to avoid air travel chaos.

text.p: The White House on Saturday said President Bill Clinton intervened to stop a pilots' strike at American Airlines to avoid travel disruptions over the Presidents Day holiday weekend and to protect the U.S. economy.

American Airlines scrambled to put its planes back in the air and passengers into its seats, offering big discounts in an effort to attract replacements for the tens of thousands of passengers who had rebooked with rival carriers.

The No. 2 U.S. carrier, a unit of Fort Worth-based AMR Corp, had almost all of its domestic flights running on schedule again on Saturday morning and was wooing travelers with a half-price sale on domestic and international flights.

Less than a half hour after a strike called "Operation Fire at Will" began at 12:01 a.m. EST (0501 GMT), Clinton jumped in to stop it. He ordered a 60-day cooling-off period by creating a presidential emergency board that has 30 days to recommend a compromise.

Management and labor will have a further 30 days to consider it. If either side rejects the board's proposed solution, the airline's 9,300 pilots could then strike. Congress would have to pass special legislation to end it.
Union leaders expressed some bitterness about the outcome.

"We may have to go another 60 days and then go out on strike a second time," James Sovich, president of the pilots' union, the Allied Pilots Association, said. "Nobody's happy about that. It's an emotional roller-coaster. We would have preferred not to do that to our members."
American Airlines management was grateful to be flying again after losing an estimated $100 million ahead of the walkout but disappointed its final offer was not accepted.

Clinton reluctantly stepped into the fray faced with the prospect of thousands of outraged travelers and losses to the U.S. economy of up to $200 million a day and to the airline of $30 million a day. It was the first presidential intervention in a U.S. airline dispute in 30 years.

"No Democratic president likes to prevent the ability of workers to strike but at the same time there were legal grounds and economic grounds for doing this, as well as the travelers who would be stranded on a holiday weekend," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, referring to the Presidents Day holiday marked in the United States on Monday.

The two sides had been trying to reach agreement on a new four-year labor contact but were unable to agree on the size of a wage increase and whether American's pilots or those of a subsidiary, American Eagle, may fly new regional jets the airline wants to buy. There was no sign of any new negotiating sessions planned and negotiators for both sides had left their Washington hotels on Saturday.

Clinton had let the clock tick on the negotiations down to the midnight deadline, hoping the two sides would reach a last-minute accord. He was watching the strike coverage on television and playing solitaire in his second-floor study in the White House when senior adviser Bruce Lindsey came in with the papers for him to sign to avert the walkout.
Lindsey told reporters later: "Hopefully we will not come to a point 60 days from now where we will be in this same situation again."
